summary.title: Bank Microservice Threat Model
summary.description: Threat model for a minimalist banking microservice with FastAPI, PostgreSQL and Redis.

data.name: Application / Infrastructure
data.description: Trust boundary separating the external user from the application and backend infrastructure.

data.name: User
data.description: External user interacting with the banking microservice through the HTTP API. The user supplies the X-User-Id header and requests account transfers and transaction history.

threats.title: User identity spoofing via X-User-Id
threats.description: The API accepts the X-User-Id HTTP header from the client and converts it directly to an integer user identifier. The supplied code does not verify the identity using JWT, OAuth2, a session or another cryptographically verifiable authentication mechanism. An attacker may therefore provide another user's identifier and act in the context of that user. This can undermine the authorization checks that rely on the user_id value.
threats.mitigation: Replace the client-controlled X-User-Id identification mechanism with proper authentication, such as OAuth2/OIDC or signed JWT access tokens. Validate the token on every protected request and derive the authenticated user ID from the verified token claims rather than from a client-supplied header. Keep server-side authorization checks for account ownership.

threats.title: Repudiation of transfer request
threats.description: The application does not show a complete audit mechanism that reliably associates transfer requests with a strongly authenticated user identity. Because the current identity is supplied through the client-controlled X-User-Id header, it may be difficult to prove which authenticated user actually initiated a transaction.
threats.mitigation: Use cryptographically verifiable authentication and derive the user identity from the verified access token. Record security-relevant events such as successful and failed transfers, authenticated user ID, source account, destination account, amount, timestamp, and transaction ID in an append-only audit log.

threats.title: Exposure of transaction history through weak identity
threats.description: GET /transactions returns the history of the account owner identified by the X-User-Id header. Because this value is supplied by the client and is not cryptographically verified, an attacker can request another user's identifier and read that user's transfers (amounts, counterparties, timestamps). This is a confidentiality breach of financial data.
threats.mitigation: Derive the user identity only from a verified token (OAuth2/OIDC or signed JWT). Add negative authorization tests (user A must not read user B's history) and log access to transaction history for monitoring.

data.name: FastAPI Backend
data.description: FastAPI backend providing the /transfer and /transactions endpoints. It receives user requests, performs authorization checks, executes database operations and uses Redis for caching.

threats.title: Unauthorized transfer due to broken authorization
threats.description: The API performs an ownership check for the source account using the user_id value obtained from the authentication layer. However, the current authentication mechanism accepts the client-controlled X-User-Id header without cryptographic verification. An attacker who can impersonate another user may therefore pass the ownership check and initiate a transfer from that user's account.
threats.mitigation: Implement strong authentication using OAuth2/OIDC or signed JWT access tokens. Derive the authenticated user ID only from a verified token and perform server-side authorization checks for every account operation. Additionally, enforce transfer limits and maintain an audit trail for financial operations.

threats.title: Replay of transfer requests
threats.description: The transfer endpoint does not show a mechanism for detecting or preventing replay of an identical request. If an attacker captures a valid transfer request, the same request may potentially be submitted again. Repeated execution could result in an unintended duplicate transfer.
threats.mitigation: Require authenticated requests using signed access tokens and implement idempotency keys for transfer operations. Store the idempotency key and resulting transaction ID for a defined period and reject duplicate requests. Log transfer attempts for auditing and investigation.

threats.title: API resource exhaustion
threats.description: The API does not show rate limiting or request throttling for transfer and transaction-history endpoints. An attacker may send a large number of requests and consume application, database, or Redis resources, potentially degrading service availability for legitimate users.
threats.mitigation: Implement rate limiting and request throttling for sensitive endpoints. Configure connection and request timeouts, limit resource consumption, monitor request rates and backend resource usage, and apply appropriate protections at the API gateway or reverse proxy.

threats.title: Race condition in transfer (double spend)
threats.description: transfer() reads the balance with a plain SELECT and then updates it in the same transaction without row locking (no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, no atomic conditional UPDATE). Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation two concurrent requests can both pass the 'Insufficient funds' check and both debit the account, producing a negative balance or an overdraft. This directly affects the integrity of the money ledger.
threats.mitigation: Lock the source row (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or use an atomic UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id=$2 AND balance >= $1; lock accounts in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks; add a CHECK (balance_cents >= 0) constraint; add concurrency tests for transfers.

threats.title: Account enumeration through error responses
threats.description: The API returns 403 for an account that exists but belongs to someone else and 404 'From/To account not found' for a missing account. An authenticated attacker can iterate account IDs and learn which accounts exist.
threats.mitigation: Return a uniform error for non-owned and non-existing source accounts; for the destination account avoid revealing existence beyond what is required; add rate limiting and monitoring of repeated failed lookups.

data.name: Cache operations
data.description: Redis GET and DELETE operations used for transaction-related cache data.

threats.title: Stale or inconsistent cache entries
threats.description: Cache keys for history have the form tx:{user_id}:{limit}:{search}, but after a transfer the code deletes only the key tx:{user_id}, which never matches the stored keys. Cached history may therefore stay stale. In addition, a cache hit currently returns an empty list. In a banking context a user may see an incorrect transaction history, and the cache can hide new transfers.
threats.mitigation: Use one consistent key scheme and invalidate with a pattern or a per-user version counter; set a short TTL; return cached data on a hit and fall back to the database on a miss; treat Redis only as a performance cache, never as a source of truth.

data.name: SQL queries
data.description: SQL queries for account ownership checks, balance updates and transaction retrieval.

threats.title: Dynamic SQL construction (potential SQL injection)
threats.description: list_transactions() builds the SQL text with f-strings (Semgrep: python-sql-dynamic-query-construction, CWE-89). Manual review shows that only the placeholder index (${i}) is interpolated, while the user-controlled value of 'search' is passed as a bound asyncpg parameter, so exploitation is NOT confirmed. The risk is regression: a future change that interpolates a value instead of a placeholder would introduce a real SQL injection. Note also that '%' and '_' in 'search' act as ILIKE wildcards.
threats.mitigation: Use a static parameterized query (e.g. ($2::text IS NULL OR ... ILIKE $2)) or a query builder instead of string concatenation; keep the Semgrep rule in CI as a regression guard; escape LIKE wildcards in user input.

data.name: HTTP API requests
data.description: Transfer requests and transaction history requests containing X-User-Id and request parameters.

threats.title: Sensitive data exposure in HTTP requests
threats.description: The client sends authentication information and transfer parameters to the FastAPI backend through HTTP API requests. If the connection is not protected with HTTPS/TLS, an attacker able to observe network traffic may capture the X-User-Id header and sensitive request data. This may expose user identity information and facilitate unauthorized access.
threats.mitigation: Use HTTPS/TLS for all client-to-API communication and redirect or reject unencrypted HTTP connections. Avoid transmitting sensitive authentication information through client-controlled headers without proper authentication. Use secure, signed access tokens and configure appropriate TLS settings.

data.name: Redis
data.description: Redis is used by the API for transaction-related cache data. It is accessed directly by the FastAPI backend.

threats.title: Unauthorized access to Redis
threats.description: Redis is used by the backend for caching and is exposed as a separate infrastructure service. The supplied configuration does not show authentication, ACLs, TLS, or network restrictions for Redis. An attacker who gains network access to the Redis service may read, modify, or delete cached data and potentially interfere with application behavior.
threats.mitigation: Restrict Redis access to the internal application network and do not expose port 6379 publicly. Enable Redis authentication and ACLs where appropriate, use TLS for connections when traffic crosses an untrusted network, and apply least-privilege access controls. Do not store sensitive data in Redis unless it is adequately protected.

threats.title: Cache data tampering
threats.description: Redis is used by the backend for application caching. An attacker with unauthorized access to Redis could modify or delete cached data. This could cause incorrect application behavior, invalidate cached information, or interfere with the availability of the service.
threats.mitigation: Restrict Redis access to the internal application network. Enable authentication and ACLs, apply least-privilege permissions, and do not expose port 6379 to untrusted networks. Validate data retrieved from the cache and ensure that sensitive operations rely on authoritative database data.

threats.title: Redis service disruption
threats.description: The FastAPI backend depends on Redis for cache operations. An attacker who can access the Redis service could delete cached data, issue excessive requests, or otherwise consume Redis resources. This could increase backend load and degrade the availability of the application.
threats.mitigation: Restrict Redis access to the internal application network and do not expose port 6379 to untrusted networks. Configure authentication and ACLs, apply resource limits, and monitor Redis availability and resource consumption. The application should also handle Redis failures gracefully without becoming unavailable.

data.name: PostgreSQL
data.description: PostgreSQL database containing accounts and transactions. Account balances and transaction records are persistent financial data.

threats.title: Unauthorized access to database
threats.description: The PostgreSQL database contains account balances and transaction records. The database service is exposed on the host through port 5432, and the deployment configuration uses a hard-coded PostgreSQL username and password. If an attacker gains network access to the exposed database service or obtains these credentials, sensitive banking data may be disclosed or modified.
threats.mitigation: Do not expose PostgreSQL directly to the host or public network unless required. Restrict database access to the application network using firewall rules and container networking. Store database credentials in secrets or environment-specific secret management instead of hard-coding them. Use a dedicated database user with only the permissions required by the application.

threats.title: Unauthorized modification of account data
threats.description: The PostgreSQL database stores account balances and transaction records. If an attacker obtains direct database access or application-level privileges beyond those required for normal operations, account balances or transaction records could be modified without authorization. Such modification could affect the integrity of financial data.
threats.mitigation: Restrict database access to the backend service and use a dedicated least-privilege database account. Do not expose PostgreSQL to untrusted networks. Apply strict authorization checks in the application and maintain audit logs for financial data changes. Protect database credentials using a secrets-management mechanism.

threats.title: Insufficient database audit trail
threats.description: The database schema contains account and transaction records but does not show a dedicated audit trail for security-sensitive database operations. Without sufficient audit logging, unauthorized or unexpected modifications to financial data may be difficult to investigate and attribute.
threats.mitigation: Implement centralized and tamper-resistant audit logging for security-sensitive operations. Record the authenticated user identity, operation, affected account or transaction, timestamp, and result. Restrict access to audit logs and retain them according to the application's security and compliance requirements.
